chapter: Billy Berg's, Granz and Nat Cole
title: Ellington's consciousness of Black heritage
summary: Callender and Willard rebut the claim that Ellington did nothing for Black musicians, citing "Black Beauty" and Jump For Joy.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: You know, you mentioned Duke and Black musicians. I heard a guy once say... I got so mad, I almost hit him. The guy said, "What did Duke Ellington ever do for Black musicians?" And they forget, or they didn't know that "Black Beauty," "Black, Brown and Beige"... Duke was conscious, well, he was never unconscious of the plight of the Black musician, or Black people.
Well, whenever he was asked to describe his music, he never described it as Jazz. He described it as "Negro music" -- when that was the term.
When that was the term. But even...
But even when it was "Negro music," he wrote "Black Beauty."
He used the term "Black Beauty" in...when was that... That was 1927 or way back there. He was always cognizant of his heritage.
Right. Which is why when people challenged him during the Civil Rights period in the Sixties, and said, "What did you ever do then?" he said,
"Well, I've been doing it all along." He did it in Jump For Joy, he said, and before that.
From the very beginning he did it.
But he did it his way.
Yeah. He just did it. He didn't make a big thing about it. That was his whole existence.
Yeah, he was expressing his heritage, his experience, and...
That's right. His experience or the Black experience. He was never that far from it, always.
